source.title: Toward A Mathematical Framework for Computation in Superposition

record.file_problem: The full post and comments are present, but some equations are flattened or malformed and figures are not reproduced.
record.tranche_reason: The post gives constructive mathematical results for computation in superposition, while refining the claim that feature readability requires near-orthogonal directions. It does not test whether ordinary trained networks or LLMs develop these representations.
record.gate_note: The post's main results are analytic constructions and bounds, not evaluations of naturally learned representations. Its discussion of loss functions, MSE feature capacity, and neuron-basis interpretations is not evidence about the claim's importance allocation or polysemanticity versions. Cited findings about LLMs and other papers are not recorded as results. An author comment describes task-trained or readout-fitted experiments, but those behaviors are purpose-induced and are not evidence of spontaneous superposition.
record.test_reason: Mostly hand-built constructions showing that computation in superposition is possible. These are purpose-built, not learned, so they are not evidence that superposition arises. Two parts do bear on V1 as a specific argument. The appendix argues that linearly readable superposed features need not be almost orthogonal in any basis. Section 2 reports small optimisation experiments where the MSE-optimal number of features stored is about O(d log d), far below what ϵ-accuracy allows. So the amount of superposition a toy model shows depends on the loss chosen.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that computation in superposition is mathematically feasible via asymptotic constructions for MLP (U-AND) and QK circuits. They say these constructions may perform poorly at finite width, error propagation across layers is unresolved, and relevance to real transformers is unclear. They also argue that ϵ-accuracy permits much more superposition than MSE minimisation, and that linear readability does not require almost-orthogonal feature vectors.
record.recipe_differences: The post gives analytic constructions for Boolean computation in MLP and QK components, rather than training the original toy-model setup to study feature storage or its sparsity transition.
record.method_sensitivity: The constructions' capacity depends on activation choice (ReLU versus quadratic), input sparsity and compositeness, the number of selected gates, and structure in the QK feature-pair set. The authors state that finite-width performance may be substantially worse than the asymptotic analysis suggests.

fits_no_version.finding: Hand-built single-layer MLP and attention QK constructions can compute many more boolean ANDs or skip feature-bigrams than they have neurons or rank, operating on superposed sparse features. Capacity is about one gate per parameter for ReLU, and superpolynomial with quadratic activations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Computation (not just storage) in superposition is feasible: networks can compute many boolean functions of sparse superposed features with fewer neurons than functions.

record.problems: The principal results are theoretical constructions, not tests of naturally learned networks or LLMs. The post says its asymptotic bounds have poor constants or logarithmic terms and may yield high interference at widths of hundreds of neurons. Error propagation across sequential layers is left open. Some QK arguments are explicitly heuristic, and the post does not provide a systematic empirical validation of the constructions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version rows were extracted from the loss-function discussion or cited findings; they do not test the versions as stated.

untested.parts: Whether trained small networks actually learn overlapping near-orthogonal storage, the sparsity-dependent phase transition, and regular geometry. The post's constructions are hand-built.
Importance-dependent allocation of dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Polysemantic neurons arising without capacity pressure. The neuron-basis description of U-AND is a conceptual argument, not a test.
Any LLM or SAE evidence. The Sam Marks XOR finding is cited only.
Completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features.
One-dimensional versus multi-dimensional features in real models.

missing.what: Empirical optimisation of a simplified toy model of superposition (1-hot inputs, hidden dim d). The MSE-optimal number of stored features is N_L2(d)=O(d log d), with N_Lp(d) curves for several p and d. The authors contrast this with exp(ϵ²d) features possible under ϵ-accuracy and argue MSE (as in the original toy models paper) understates possible superposition. The verdict on V1 relies partly on this from the text.
missing.locator: Section 2, 'What are the implications of using ϵ-accuracy?', figure 'Experimental values of NLp(d)'

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked R1–R6 to V1 as 'supports'. But these are purpose-built constructions and say nothing about whether superposition arises in trained networks, so they are moved to fits_no_version. Comment-thread experiments (training on U-AND, readouts over a frozen random layer) involve task-induced training and are excluded. The post appears to be a precursor of arXiv:2408.05451.

versions.untested_parts: The post establishes feasibility for specified constructions; it does not test whether trained networks learn them, test an empirical sparsity-dependent transition, or test feature importance.
No test of importance-dependent dedication or sharing of dimensions among features.
The neuron-basis discussion is not a test of polysemantic neurons arising through other mechanisms in models.
No empirical test in LLMs or SAE feature recovery.
No test of whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical.
The constructions use vector-valued features, but the post does not test whether features in real models are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: ReLU U-AND construction (not named)
rows.size_stated: Input dimension d0; hidden width d, with d = ω(log^8 d0)
rows.operation_detail: Analytically construct a sparse random-weight ReLU layer and linear read-offs for every pairwise AND of orthogonal input features.
rows.measure: Number of pairwise ANDs represented and read-off error
rows.value: The construction represents Θ(d0^2) pairwise ANDs with a d-neuron layer; stated error is ϵ = O(1/log^2(d0)).
rows.note: A constructive existence result. The output AND features are represented using normalized intersections of neuron subsets, which the post says are almost orthogonal.
rows.check: Hand-designed U-AND construction (purpose-built weights). It shows that computing ANDs in superposition is feasible, not that small networks store features this way. Not a test of V1.

rows.subject: Targeted superpositional ReLU U-AND construction (not named)
rows.size_stated: Input dimension d0; hidden width d; m may be superpolynomial in d0
rows.operation_detail: Construct sparse connections tailored to a selected set E of feature pairs, assigning neurons to gates.

conditions.value: m random feature vectors in superposition
Inputs have a constant-bounded number of active features

rows.measure: Number of selected pairwise AND gates represented
rows.value: The construction can compute up to about ~Θ(d0d) selected ANDs while keeping each neuron connected to at most d0 input features.
rows.locator: Section 1.3, “A construction which computes a subset of ANDs of inputs in superposition”
rows.note: The post presents this as an analytic construction; it does not report training or a learned network.
rows.check: Hand-designed targeted-AND construction. It is a feasibility and capacity bound for the authors' own construction, not a measurement of learned representations.

rows.subject: ReLU U-AND construction with superposed inputs (not named)
rows.size_stated: Input dimension d0; hidden width d
rows.operation_detail: Derive the scale at which random-vector interference causes neurons to misfire in the basic superpositional construction.
rows.measure: Feature count at misfiring threshold and pairwise AND count
rows.value: Neurons start to misfire when m = ~Θ(d0√d); at this point the number of pairwise ANDs is ~Θ(d0^2d).
rows.locator: Section 1.3, “Construction details for inputs in superposition”
rows.note: This is a stated asymptotic limitation of the basic construction, not a measurement of a trained model.
rows.check: A limitation (misfiring threshold) of the authors' own construction, not a result on V1. The 'partial' state against V1 is not meaningful.

rows.subject: Quadratic-activation U-AND construction (not named)
rows.operation_detail: Construct a single-layer quadratic-activation map with linear read-offs for pairwise ANDs of sparse feature vectors.

conditions.value: ϵ-almost-orthogonal vectors embedded in an r-dimensional subspace

rows.measure: Number of features accommodated and AND read-off error
rows.value: The post states that the construction handles a number of features exponential in √d (superpolynomial in d), with read-off error O(s^2ϵ) for sparsity s.
rows.note: This is a constructive result using one-dimensional feature vectors; it is not a test of learned feature geometry.
rows.check: Hand-designed quadratic-activation construction. It is a capacity result for a built circuit, not for learned feature storage.

rows.subject: Low-rank QK skip-feature-bigram construction (not named)
rows.size_stated: Matrix rank at most dhead; residual dimension dresid
rows.operation_detail: Construct a low-rank attention bilinear form for a generic selected set of skip feature-bigrams using random projection.
rows.measure: Number of bigrams checked with signal larger than interference
rows.value: The post gives a capacity of up to ~Θ(dresid dhead) bigrams, up to logarithmic factors, with the stated additional condition that no feature occurs in more than ~Θ(dhead) bigrams.
rows.note: The post describes this as a heuristic analytic argument for the construction.
rows.check: Heuristic capacity argument for a constructed low-rank QK matrix. It concerns computation (bigram checking), not feature storage in toy networks.

rows.subject: Structured-clique QK construction (not named)
rows.size_stated: Residual dimension dresid; attention rank dhead
rows.operation_detail: Represent cliques of skip feature-bigrams using rank-one tensors formed from sums of feature vectors.

conditions.value: At most dhead cliques; balanced clique sizes

rows.value: The post derives up to dresid^2 bigrams across dhead cliques in the balanced case, and up to dhead dresid in the stated one-sided case.
rows.note: The achievable count depends on structure in the set of feature pairs.
rows.check: Constructed structured-clique QK circuit. It is not a measurement of learned representations.

rows.subject: Bundled linearly readable feature-vector construction (not named)
rows.size_stated: Dimension d; number of vectors described asymptotically in the appendix
rows.operation_detail: Give a probabilistic construction of feature vectors that are linearly readable but not almost orthogonal in any basis.

conditions.value: Bundles of vectors formed from a shared random vector plus small independent perturbations
The post gives read-off vectors for the individual features

rows.measure: Linear readability and existence of a basis making vectors almost orthogonal
rows.value: The post states that the features can be read off with error o(1), while with high probability there is no basis in which the vectors are almost unit and almost orthogonal to error 1/10.
rows.locator: Appendix, “Linear readability and its consequences”; Appendix to the appendix
rows.note: This qualifies near-orthogonality as a sufficient constructional geometry, not a necessary consequence of linear readability.
rows.check: A mathematical counterexample, not a trained network. It bears on V1's geometry part: superposed features can be linearly readable (error o(1)) yet have no basis where they are almost orthogonal (error 1/10). So near-orthogonality is sufficient, not necessary, for superposition. Subject kind is a constructed vector set, not a toy network.

source_check.correct: The post states readability with error o(1). Its no-basis argument requires transformed feature vectors to be almost unit length, or to have norms between fixed nonzero constants. Without a norm requirement, the corresponding angular near-orthogonality counterexample is conjectured, not established.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix, Linear readability and its consequences, text lines 710–712; Appendix to the appendix, lines 724–756.
source_check.problem: The row omits the norm restriction needed for the stated no-basis result.

relation.reason: The geometric counterexample and loss comparison bear directly on qualifications to V1, although they do not demonstrate that trained networks adopt these constructions.

tranche.reason: The appendix provides a specific argument qualifying the necessity of near-orthogonal geometry; Section 2 also argues that permissible superposition depends on the reconstruction objective.

source_check.notes: The geometric result is presented as a proof sketch. The loss-comparison result has no listed row; neither it nor the bundled construction establishes that gradient training realizes the specific theoretical solutions.

statements.correction: Bundled vectors are linearly readable with error o(1). With high probability, no basis makes them simultaneously almost unit and almost orthogonal at error 1/10; the argument also extends to norms bounded between fixed nonzero constants. The unrestricted angular version is conjectured. Training realization of the bundled construction is not demonstrated.
statements.problem: The bundled-vector claim omits the transformed-vector norm restriction. The post does not establish impossibility of angular near-orthogonality with unrestricted norms.
